detail.scope: Commercial-sector electricity sales and average price by state, as reported to EIA. Data centers are billed mostly in the commercial class, so this is a proxy for their load, not a measurement of it.

analysis.body:
The five grid operators represented here — ERCOT, NYISO, MISO, SPP, and CAISO — collectively show more than 1.3 million megawatts of generation and storage projects waiting in interconnection queues as of August 31, 2026, spread across roughly 8,381 individual requests. These are planned projects that have asked to connect to the grid, not operating capacity and not data center demand directly; a large share will be withdrawn or delayed before they ever run. Still, the composition of what developers are queuing tells a story about where grid builders expect future load. ERCOT, which covers most of Texas, leads with 440,018 MW across 1,797 requests, with storage at roughly 160,906 MW and gas at 76,751 MW standing out alongside solar; those fuel mixes — particularly the pairing of large-scale storage with dispatchable gas — are consistent with serving the kind of always-on, high-density load that data centers require, though the queue itself cannot confirm that is the driver.

Looking across the other operators, CAISO's active queue of 71,682 MW is the smallest by total volume but carries the highest storage share proportionally, with 46,944 MW of storage against only 916 MW of gas among its 265 active requests, reflecting California's policy environment as much as any demand signal. MISO's 299,721 MW queue across 3,827 requests is dominated by solar at nearly 144,902 MW and wind at 51,746 MW, while its storage figure of 68,429 MW and gas of 30,236 MW suggest a different regional load profile than Texas. SPP shows 199,215 MW with gas at 47,392 MW and storage at 53,412 MW, the highest gas-to-total ratio outside ERCOT. NYISO's 319,095 MW queue is notable for its "other" category of 291,136 MW, which reflects how that operator classifies certain project types and is not directly comparable to fuel-specific breakdowns from the other sources. The commercial electricity sales data from EIA, covering June 2026, shows Texas with the highest reported commercial-sector sales at 15,754 gigawatt-hours and the lowest average price at $8.66 per megawatt-hour among the states listed, while California's 10,025 GWh comes at $27.33 — a price spread that, combined with queue size, helps explain why so much interconnection activity is concentrated in the ERCOT footprint.

What matters for AI infrastructure observers is not any single queue number but the trajectory of storage and gas additions, which serve as rough proxies for load-following capacity of the kind data centers need; watch whether ERCOT's gas queue additions continue to grow in future monthly Generator Interconnection Status reports, as sustained increases there would suggest developers are responding to firm, round-the-clock demand rather than purely policy-driven renewable buildout.
